opening: Our app sends a lot of push notifications and more people are turning them off. Design a system that decides which notifications to send.

clarifications.answer: Billions of candidate notifications a day from likes, comments, follows, friend posts, recommendations and reminders.
Each candidate can be sent as a push, kept in the in-app inbox only, or dropped.
The goal is long-term engagement; opt-outs, disabled notifications and uninstalls are the main costs.
Sending at the wrong time annoys people; users are spread across many time zones and some set quiet hours.
Security alerts and direct messages must always be delivered promptly; everything else is optional.
We log every notification sent, opened, dismissed or followed by an opt-out, plus app activity times.

clarificationPolicy: Answer as the notifications product lead. Keep it a high-volume decision problem with long-term costs and timing; decide unlisted details so uplift framing, budgets and long-term measurement stay central.

agenda.goal: Establish volume, decisions available, costs and must-send cases.
agenda.opener: What would you like to know before designing this?

evidence.strong: Asks about users and candidate volume, the options (push, inbox, drop), the goal and the cost of opt-outs, timing and quiet hours, and which notifications must always go out.
evidence.adequate: Gets volume but not the cost of sending.
evidence.weak: Assumes every notification should be sent.

misconceptions.pattern: Assumes more notifications mean more engagement.
misconceptions.challenge: If someone gets thirty pushes a day, what do they eventually do?

probes: What does sending one too many cost?
hints: Every push spends some of the user's patience.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Billions of optional candidates for hundreds of millions of users, push versus inbox versus drop, opt-outs as the cost, timing matters, and transactional alerts always sent.

agenda.goal: Lay out the pipeline from events to delivered notifications.
agenda.opener: Walk me through how an event becomes a notification on someone's phone.

evidence.strong: Producers emit candidates to a queue, an aggregator dedupes and batches similar events, a decision service scores and applies budgets, a scheduler holds items for the chosen send time, and a delivery service sends through push providers with retries; transactional alerts bypass ranking.
evidence.adequate: A model and a sender with no aggregation or scheduling.
evidence.weak: Every event sends a push immediately.

misconceptions.challenge: Fifty people like a photo in ten minutes. How many pushes does the owner get?

probes: Where do you combine similar events?
How do urgent alerts avoid waiting behind ranking?
hints: Not everything should go through the same path.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Candidates queued, aggregated and deduplicated, scored with budgets, scheduled, and delivered with retries; transactional alerts bypass ranking.

agenda.goal: Frame the decision as the value of sending versus not sending.
agenda.opener: What exactly should a model predict to decide whether to send?

evidence.strong: Predicts the incremental effect of sending (uplift on sessions) and the risk of opt-out or uninstall, combining them into a value; notes that high open probability may reflect people who would open the app anyway; trains with randomised holdouts.
evidence.adequate: Predicts open probability and adds an opt-out penalty.

misconceptions.pattern: Sends notifications with the highest predicted open rate.
misconceptions.challenge: Someone opens the app every hour anyway. Does a push to them add anything?

probes: How do you know a notification caused the visit?
How do you put a cost on an opt-out?
hints: Compare with what would have happened without the push.
Some costs show up weeks later.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Predict the uplift of sending and the opt-out risk, combine into a value, and learn from randomised holdouts.

agenda.goal: Limit volume per user and choose the best few.
agenda.opener: A user has thirty candidates today. How many do they get, and which ones?

evidence.strong: A per-user daily budget learned from tolerance, candidates competing for slots by value, fatigue features (recent volume, recent dismissals), lower-value items moved to the inbox, and counters in a fast store.

misconceptions.challenge: Ten notifications each look worth sending. Together are they still worth it?

probes: Should every user have the same cap?
What happens to notifications that don't make the cut?
hints: People differ in how many they tolerate.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Per-user learned budgets, competition by value, fatigue features, and inbox fallback for lower-value items.

agenda.goal: Send at times people are likely to welcome it.
agenda.opener: When should a notification be sent?

evidence.strong: Uses each user's activity pattern and time zone to choose a send window, respects quiet hours, keeps time-sensitive items immediate, uses a scheduler with delayed jobs, and re-checks relevance at send time.

misconceptions.pattern: Thinks sending immediately is always best.
misconceptions.challenge: A friend posts at 3 am your time. Should your phone buzz?

probes: What if the item is no longer relevant when the window comes?
hints: Learn when each person usually uses the app.
Re-validate before delivering a delayed item.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Per-user send windows from activity and time zone, quiet hours, immediate time-sensitive items, and re-validation at send time.

agenda.goal: Measure long-term effects, not just short-term lifts.
agenda.opener: How would you know a change is good for the product over months?

evidence.strong: A long-running holdout with fewer or no optional notifications, tracking retention, notification-disable and uninstall rates alongside sessions; warns that sending more lifts short-term metrics while eroding long-term engagement.
evidence.adequate: An A/B test on daily sessions for a week or two.

misconceptions.pattern: Trusts a two-week lift in sessions.
misconceptions.challenge: Sending twice as many pushes lifts sessions for two weeks. What could happen in month three?

probes: What metric would reveal slow damage?
Why keep some users with fewer notifications for a long time?
hints: A holdout shows the true long-term effect.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Long-running holdouts tracking retention, disables and uninstalls alongside sessions.

agenda.goal: Deliver reliably at very high volume.
agenda.opener: How do the chosen notifications actually get delivered at this scale?

evidence.strong: A delivery service with queues per provider, respect for provider rate limits, retries with backoff, dead-letter handling, device token management (removing invalid tokens), idempotency to avoid duplicates, and delivery and open receipts fed back to logs.
evidence.adequate: Sends through a provider with retries.
evidence.weak: Calls the provider synchronously from the decision service.

misconceptions.challenge: The provider timed out after actually sending. What does the user see after your retry?

probes: What happens to tokens for uninstalled apps?
How do you avoid sending the same push twice?
agenda.moveOnSummary: Per-provider queues within rate limits, retries with backoff, dead letters, token hygiene, idempotency, and receipts back to logs.

agenda.goal: Combine low-value events into fewer, richer notifications.
agenda.opener: How would you handle a burst of small events for one person?

evidence.strong: Groups similar events in a short window per user and type into one notification ('Asha and 12 others liked your photo'), with a digest option for low-value types, implemented as windowed aggregation in a stream job.

misconceptions.pattern: Treats every event as its own notification.
misconceptions.challenge: A post goes viral and gets thousands of likes. What happens to the author's phone?

probes: How long do you wait before sending an aggregate?
Which types suit a daily digest?
hints: A short window collects related events.
Some updates can wait for a summary.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Windowed per-user aggregation into summary notifications and digests for low-value types.

evidence.strong: Short-term sessions versus long-term trust, immediacy versus better timing, personalised budgets versus simplicity, and measurement cost of holdouts.

probes: What would you never trade away?
hints: A disabled notification channel is hard to win back.
Holdouts cost some engagement to learn.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Short-term lift versus long-term trust, immediacy versus timing, and personalisation versus simplicity.

curveballs.prompt: The growth team doubled notification volume last quarter and sessions went up. Now opt-outs are climbing. How would you settle the argument?
A user's post goes viral overnight and they wake up to hundreds of notifications. What should have happened?

alternatives.choice: Contextual bandits choosing whether and when to send
alternatives.whenBetter: When fast online learning matters and the team can log propensities for evaluation.

alternatives.choice: Rule-based caps and priorities with no model
alternatives.whenBetter: For a small app or as a launch baseline before outcome data exists.

alternatives.choice: Daily digests instead of individual pushes for most types
alternatives.whenBetter: When most notifications are low-urgency and fatigue is high.

exemplars.label: Uplift with budgets and holdouts
exemplars.outline: Clarifies volume, push versus inbox versus drop, opt-outs as the cost, timing and must-send alerts. Queues candidates, aggregates bursts into summaries, scores the uplift of sending and opt-out risk learned from randomised holdouts, allocates per-user budgets with fatigue features, picks send times from activity and time zones with quiet hours, and delivers through rate-limited, idempotent provider queues with retries. Transactional alerts bypass ranking. Measures with long-running holdouts on retention, disables and uninstalls.

exemplars.label: Open-rate model with a cap
exemplars.outline: Predicts open probability per notification, sends those above a threshold with a fixed daily cap and time-zone check, and A/B tests sessions for two weeks; no uplift framing, aggregation or long-term holdout.

exemplars.label: Send everything
exemplars.outline: Sends a push for every event immediately and lets users disable types in settings; no model, budget or measurement.
